Achaicus
uh-KAY-i-kus
proper noun (figure)
Greek/Latin Achaicus ("belonging to Achaia, a man of Achaia"), from the Roman province of Achaia (southern Greece). A common name, sometimes given to a slave from that region. One of three Corinthians who refreshed Paul's spirit (1 Cor 16:17).

📖 Biblical Definition

Achaicus was a Christian at Corinth who, with Stephanas and Fortunatus, came to the Apostle Paul and refreshed his spirit, as recorded in the closing of 1 Corinthians: "I am glad of the coming of Stephanas and Fortunatus and Achaicus: for that which was lacking on your part they have supplied. For they have refreshed my spirit and yours: therefore acknowledge ye them that are such" (1 Cor 16:17-18). His name means "a man of Achaia," the Roman province of southern Greece in which Corinth lay; such regional names were sometimes given to slaves identified by their place of origin, suggesting Achaicus may have been a freedman or slave. He is named together with Fortunatus (another humble Roman name) and Stephanas (whose household was the firstfruits of Achaia), and the three appear to have formed a delegation from the Corinthian church to Paul, likely carrying the letter to which 1 Corinthians is in part a reply, and supplying in person what the distance had left lacking. Achaicus shares fully in the honor Paul gives the three: they refreshed his spirit, and the church is commanded to acknowledge such men. Of his particular character, deeds, or later life, Scripture says nothing — he is one of the obscure faithful, named for a single, valued service. He stands, with Quartus, Fortunatus, and the other named brethren, for the great company of ordinary believers whose service to Christ and to His servants the Spirit of God saw fit to record in the permanent Word, that the church might honor them and learn from them the grace of practical, refreshing, self-giving service.

A Corinthian believer who, with Stephanas and Fortunatus, came to Paul and refreshed his spirit (1 Cor 16:17-18); his name means "a man of Achaia," suggesting humble origin; one of the obscure faithful named for a single valued service.

ACHAICUS, proper noun. Greek/Latin Achaicus ("a man of Achaia"); a regional name, sometimes of slaves.

A Christian of Corinth, named once: 1 Cor 16:17, with Stephanas and Fortunatus.

The three came to Paul, supplied what was lacking, and refreshed his spirit (1 Cor 16:17-18).

His name (from the province of Achaia) suggests humble or servile origin.

One of the obscure faithful, named for a single valued service; the church is told to acknowledge such men.

📖 Key Scripture

1 Corinthians 16:17-18 — "I am glad of the coming of Stephanas and Fortunatus and Achaicus: for that which was lacking on your part they have supplied. For they have refreshed my spirit and yours: therefore acknowledge ye them that are such."

1 Corinthians 16:15 — "Ye know the house of Stephanas, that it is the firstfruits of Achaia, and that they have addicted themselves to the ministry of the saints."

Philippians 2:29-30 — "Receive him therefore in the Lord with all gladness; and hold such in reputation: Because for the work of Christ he was nigh unto death, not regarding his life, to supply your lack of service toward me."

Hebrews 6:10 — "For God is not unrighteous to forget your work and labour of love, which ye have shewed toward his name, in that ye have ministered to the saints, and do minister."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Achaicus is corrupted only when the obscure faithful are despised — when the church values the prominent and forgets that the Spirit recorded the names of humble servants who refreshed the apostle and ministered to the saints.

expand to see more

Obscure-faithful despised. Achaicus is one of the many believers in Scripture known by a single mention and a single service. The instinct of the fallen heart, and of much of church culture, is to honor the prominent and overlook the obscure. Scripture rebukes the instinct: "God is not unrighteous to forget your work and labour of love, which ye have shewed toward his name, in that ye have ministered to the saints" (Heb 6:10). Achaicus ministered to the saints and to the apostle; God did not forget it, but recorded his name in the permanent Word. The church that learns from Achaicus learns to value the humble servant as God values him.

Achaicus has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal point worth recovering is the dignity Scripture gives to obscure, practical, self-giving service. Achaicus, of humble name and no recorded office, refreshed the spirit of the apostle and ministered to the saints, and is named forever for it. Like Quartus the brother and Fortunatus the refresher, he stands for the great company of ordinary believers whose labour of love God does not forget (Heb 6:10).
